narrativeContexts.context: Application deployment on OpenShift progresses from manual GUI operations through CLI scripting to fully automated GitOps workflows with AI-assisted self-service capabilities provided by Developer Hub and OpenShift Lightspeed.

narratives.name: Scalability Maturity
narratives.description: Application scalability progression on OpenShift

narrativeContexts.context: Application scalability on OpenShift evolves from manual replica adjustment through policy-based automation to predictive optimization with cost awareness using HorizontalPodAutoscalers, ClusterAutoscaler, and ClusterResourceOverride operators.

Define resource requests and limits first to enable proper scheduling; implement HorizontalPodAutoscaler with appropriate metrics (CPU, memory, or custom); enable ClusterAutoscaler for elastic node capacity; mature to predictive analytics for proactive optimization based on historical patterns.

Setting resource requests far below actual usage causes constant scaling to maximum replicas; overly aggressive scaling policies cause replica count flapping; neglecting Pod Disruption Budgets risks availability during scale-down operations.

narrativeContexts.context: Application resilience on OpenShift matures from basic health probes through graceful degradation patterns to comprehensive SRE practices with error budget tracking and chaos engineering validation.

Implement liveness and readiness probes first with appropriate timeouts; add circuit breakers, retry logic, and graceful termination; centralize observability signals (logs, metrics, traces); adopt SRE practices with SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, and toil reduction.

Using same probe for liveness and readiness causes cascading failures during high load; missing timeout configurations allows request queueing; cause-based alerting generates excessive noise without actionable insights; neglecting error budgets prevents data-driven reliability decisions.

narratives.name: Platform Context
narratives.description: OpenShift platform infrastructure architecture and evolution

narrativeContexts.context: OpenShift platform infrastructure builds on enterprise Kubernetes with Red Hat's hardened operating system (RHCOS), integrated GitOps, and operator-driven automation. Platform engineers architect high availability control planes, security-hardened network isolation, and multi-cluster fleet management to deliver resilient foundation for cloud-native workloads.

Key platform concepts include the immutable RHCOS operating system, CRI-O container runtime, etcd distributed key-value store for cluster state, and the operator pattern for automated lifecycle management. Private clusters isolate API endpoints from public internet while bastion hosts control administrative SSH access.

Architectural decisions include minimum three-node control planes for quorum-based fault tolerance, dedicated infrastructure nodes separating platform services from application workloads, and multi-zone deployment for geographic resilience. GitOps with Argo CD eliminates manual cluster configuration drift, and Machine Operator enables remote management without SSH access. Multi-cluster evolution leverages Advanced Cluster Management for centralized policy enforcement, observability aggregation, and disaster recovery orchestration.

Success depends on treating infrastructure as code through GitOps, replacing manual operations with versioned software, and systematically eliminating toil through automation investment aligned with SRE principles.

narrativeContexts.context: OpenShift persistent storage decouples data lifecycle from pod lifecycle, enabling stateful applications like databases, message queues, and file servers. Storage infrastructure maturity progresses from manual pre-provisioning through self-service dynamic allocation to distributed storage systems with cross-cluster capabilities.

Core storage concepts include PersistentVolumes (PV) as cluster-level storage resources, PersistentVolumeClaims (PVC) as application-level storage requests, StorageClasses as dynamic provisioning templates, and Container Storage Interface (CSI) drivers as the standard plugin mechanism for storage backends.

Static provisioning requires administrators to manually create PersistentVolume resources matched to PersistentVolumeClaims, suitable for initial adoption but limiting agility. Dynamic provisioning via StorageClasses enables self-service volume allocation with technology-specific parameters. Advanced storage services like OpenShift Data Foundation provide Ceph-based distributed storage with multi-zone replication, snapshots, clones, and encryption at rest. Hybrid cloud evolution spans on-premises and cloud with object storage integration and cross-cluster migration capabilities.

Success depends on selecting appropriate storage technologies for workload characteristics, implementing monitoring and alerting on capacity and performance, and protecting data through snapshots and disaster recovery procedures.

narrativeContexts.context: OpenShift networking defaults to allowing all pod-to-pod communication, creating a large attack surface if a pod is compromised. NetworkPolicy resources restrict traffic to only required flows, embodying zero-trust networking principles.

Begin by understanding application communication requirements through traffic analysis or architecture documentation. Start with deny-by-default baseline by creating NetworkPolicy with empty ingress array, then create additive policies permitting specific flows using label selectors. Always permit DNS traffic to kube-dns on port 53.

Test policies in non-production before applying to production, as overly restrictive rules can break applications. Monitor NetworkPolicy behavior using flow logs and document policies alongside deployment manifests in Git for GitOps workflows.

narrativeContexts.context: Cryptographic signing with Sigstore ensures only verified, attested artifacts are deployed, protecting against supply chain attacks by validating artifact provenance and integrity.

Deploy Trusted Artifact Signer operator. Configure CI/CD pipelines to sign images and generate SBOM and provenance attestations. Store signatures in Rekor transparency log. Define ImagePolicy resources. Configure admission webhook to validate signatures before pod creation.
Key management is critical; use hardware security modules or cloud KMS for signing key protection. Ensure Rekor is highly available to prevent deployment outages.

Install Compliance Operator from OperatorHub. Create ScanSettingBinding resources specifying compliance profiles. Schedule scans automatically. Review ComplianceCheckResult objects. Apply ComplianceRemediation resources. Export reports for audit.
Not all compliance checks can be automatically remediated; manual review and risk acceptance processes are required for exceptions.

Enable etcd encryption with key rotation, configure dedicated VPC with firewall rules, integrate OAuth with enterprise IdP, automate certificate rotation, remove kube-admin account, separate infrastructure nodes.
